Description: Creates a new group or adds a given user to an existing group.
Creates a new user.
Extracts or lists files from a given .a, .ar or .lib archive.
Reports the computer's processor architecture. For example, "i486", "i686", "x86_64", etc.
An x86 assembler and the default backend of GCC.
Prints a table containing all 128 ASCII characters. For each character, its decimal (Dec) and hexadecimal (Hex) values are displayed with it.
An AWK processor. AWK is a scripting language designed for text pattern scanning and processing and useful for data extraction and reporting.
Encodes text to Base32 or decodes Base32 to text from a file to standard output.
Encodes text to Base64 or decodes Base64 to text from a file to standard output.

Extracts the file name and/or the extension from a given path. If just a directory path is given, it will extract both. If a file extension is also given, it will extract the extension in addition to the directory path if it matches. For example, running "basename /etc/resolv.conf" will return "resolv.conf"; running "basename /etc/resolv.conf .conf" will return "resolv".

An arbitrary precision calculator and language. It launches into an interactive mode that allows you to enter expressions, with an optional math library for functions like sqrt and sin, or you pipe an expression via standard input to get an immediate, non-interactive result.

Allows you to produce a tone or a chain of tones using the PC speaker. You can set the frequency (Hz), length (ms), delay before playing (ms) and how many times it should repeat, and chain multiple tones together in a single command.
Prints the universally unique identifier (UUID) and filesystem type for all found filesystems or for a given partition.
Decompresses given bzip2 archives, or bzip2-compressed standard input to standard output. By default, it will replace the input files unless told otherwise.
Decompresses a given bzip2 archive to standard output. Functions like bunzip2 -c.
Compresses given files or standard input into a bzip2 archive. By default, it will replace the input files unless told otherwise.
Used for concatenating (combining) files, providing a standard output for printing or writing to a file. When its output is not directed, it prints the result.
Changes the group owner of any given files with the given group name or ID.

Changes one or more file mode bits of any given files, either with an octal number representing the mode's bit pattern or symbolic representations for a specific change. It changes how files can be accessed - can it be read, written, or executed as a program.
Changes the user and/or group owner of any given files to the given user and group names or IDs.
Changes user passwords based on standard input. Compared to passwd, this is intended for script/batch processing usage.

Runs a given program that believes the root directory is any directory of your choice. It is useful for rescue and sandboxing, allowing you to run a program that cannot make changes outside the given directory.

Changes the active virtual terminal. Changing the current virtual terminal is useful for terminal-based multi-tasking, troubleshooting and recovery. It functions similarly to pressing Ctrl+Alt+[F1/F2/F3/etc.]
Clears the terminal so that the cursor is positioned at the top. It is similar to "cls" on MS-DOS, Microsoft Windows, etc.
Lists or extracts files from a cpio archive on standard input, creates an archive from a list of files from standard input, or copies files from a list of files from standard input.
Allows you to manage your crontab, a way of scheduling recurring jobs with the cron daemon (crond). You can list, edit and delete the current crontab, or replace it with the contents of a given file.

Prints a hash for the given or prompted password. You can optionally specify the encryption type (DES, MD5, SHA256, SHA512 and yescrypt) and specify a salt to add some 'randomness' to the hash. This BusyBox implementation functions the same as mkpasswd.

An interactive C and C++ source code browser. It builds a symbol database from a given project's source files, letting you quickly jump to where a function or variable is defined, called or referenced elsewhere in the codebase.
A multi-language source code object indexing tool that generates tags files that allow editors such as Emacs, vi and Vim to jump straight to a definition of a function, variable or other symbol.
Deletes the given group or removes the given user from the given group.
Deletes the given user.

Allows you to create and display dialog boxes from a shell script. dialog includes the following boxes: buildlist, calendar, checklist, dselect, editbox, form, fselect, gauge, infobox, inputbox, inputmenu, menu, mixedform, mixedgauge, msgbox, passwordbox, passwordform, pause, prgbox, programbox, progressbox, radiolist, rangebox, tailbox, tailboxbg, textbox, timebox, treeview and yesno. The SHORK 486 Build Configurator is dialog based, and the Linux kernel's lxdialog is a distant descendant of dialog.
Compares two files line-by-line and outputs a difference listing between them. The result can be used as a patch file for the patch utility.
Converts a text file from using DOS-style line breaks (carriage return + line feed) to using Unix-style line breaks (line feed).
A DOS emulator.
Opens the Vim editor in line-orientated mode. It processes commands line-by-line rather than providing a full interactive experience.

Preallocates disk space for a file without writing data to it. It is useful for reserving space for something without needing to write zeros or random data (as you would with dd) - for example, creating swap files, preallocating space for a database or log, or testing behaviour with large files.
Identifies and reports the type of data contained in a file.

Reports the amount of total, used and free system physical memory and (if available) swap memory, largely acting as a frontend to /proc/meminfo. It produces a table containing the total (MemTotal/SwapTotal), used (total - available), free (MemFree/SwapFree), shared (Shmem), buffers (Buffers) + cache (Cached/SReclaimable), and available (MemAvailable) memory. All values are in kibibytes (KiB).
An FTP client for remote file transfer.
Lists the process IDs that have the given file or network port open. It can also be told to directly kill or send a signal to the matched processes.
GCC's C++ compiler.
GCC's C compiler (configured to use musl).

Gets an extended attribute from the given filesystem object. Extended attributes are metadata that go beyond the standard attributes provided by the host filesystem, allowing more information to be associated with a given filesystem object.
Opens a TTY and prompts for a login, accepting a user name before invoking the login command to complete the rest of the login cycle.
GCC's Fortran compiler.
A distributed version control software system.
Virtual console mouse.
Decompresses given gzip archives, or gzip-compressed standard input to standard output. By default, it will replace the input files unless told otherwise.
Compresses given files or standard input into a gzip archive. By default, it will replace the input files unless told otherwise.

An interactive process viewer designed to be an enhancement over top. Compared to top, htop supports scrolling both horizontally and vertically, a coloured UI and colour-coding, CPU and memory usage bars, searching, filtering, sorting, and killing processes.
Prints the current user's user ID, primary group ID, and any supplementary group IDs the user is a part of.

A C code formatter. It can format a given C source file to a desired indentation and styling rule (GNU style by default), or convert between different C formatting conventions (for example, from GNU style to K&R style).
A WordStar-style text editor.
A command-line JSON processor.

Sends a signal to the process that matches the given process ID. By default, it will try to gracefully terminate the process, but a given signal number (such as 9 for an immediate kill) can be given as well.
Sends a signal to all processes with a given name. By default, it will try to gracefully terminate the process, but a given signal number (such as 9 for an immediate kill) can be given as well.
Displays the contents of a file in the terminal, allowing it to be scrolled line-by-line. It uses vi-style keybinds.

Creates a hard or symbolic link to a given target file or directory. Hard links are files that point to the same inode as the target file, which must be within the same file system, and hard links to directories are generally not supported. Symbolic links are files that point to the target file or directory, which can be on another file system and even target a non-existent file/directory. Deleting the target of a hard link will not delete the data so long as at least one hard link to it exists; deleting the target of a symbolic link will break the link.
Shows a login prompt and creates a new user session once completed. If a user was already logged in, their session will be replaced upon login's completion.
Prints the current user's name. Functions similarly to whoami but uses utmp as its source.
Lists the contents of the current or a target directory.
Linux Standard Base/distribution info reporter.

Lists information about all or the specified block devices. By default, it produces a table containing the device name, major number (driver associated with device), minor number (device number for the given driver), device type, whether the device is read only (RO), and its mountpoint (if mounted).
Lists all files presently opened on the system, showing which processes have what open.

Lists all PCI buses and connected devices. By default, it produces a table containing the PCI bus number, device number for that bus, function number, PCI class code, vendor ID, and device ID. It can optionally also display the kernel driver utilising a given device.
Lists all USB buses and connected devices. It produces a table containing the USB bus number, device number for that bus, vendor ID, and device ID.
A text-based web browser that allows you to access websites from your terminal. It is the oldest web browser that is still actively maintained.
Decompresses a given LZMA archive to standard output. Functions like unlzma -c.

Decompresses given LZMA archives, or LZMA-compressed standard input to standard output. By default, it will replace the input files unless told otherwise. Note: unlike XZ Utils' implementation of lzma, BusyBox's version cannot compress any input.
Compresses given files or standard input into a LZO archive.
Decompresses a given LZO archive to standard output. Functions like unlzop -c.

A build automation tool that executes shell commands primarily to update program compilation targets only when their prerequisites have changed, avoiding unnecessary work. It is often run in the same directory as a Makefile, which describes how a project's files relate to each other and how to update them. Whilst it is often associated with C-language projects, Make can be used for any task where maintaining some files in a project can be done with shell commands, whether it be other programming languages or documentation generation, asset pipelines or general project automation.
Norton Commander-style file manager.
A userspace memory subsystem fault tester.
A text editor with Emacs-style keybinds and buffers.

A Python implementation intended for microcontrollers, embedded systems and other constrained platforms. It implements Python 3.4 syntax with select keywords and features from later versions. It is capable of installing and managing mip modules from micropython-lib.
Creates a directory at the given directory path or in the current directory with a given name without a path.
Creates a FAT32 file system on the given device or image file. The device or image will be readable with Windows 95 OSR2 or newer.
Creates an ext2 file system on the given device or image file.

Prints a hash for the given or prompted password. You can optionally specify the encryption type (DES, MD5, SHA256, SHA512 and yescrypt) and specify a salt to add some 'randomness' to the hash. This BusyBox implementation functions the same as cryptpw.
Used to set up a Linux swap area on a given partition or file. It will destroy any data present on the target partition or file.
A free MP3 player designed to be a drop-in replacement for the non-free mpg123.
Controls a magnetic tape drive. It provides typical drive operations such as rewinding, skipping and ejecting.
A Pico-style text editor.

A portable x86 assembler. Compared to GNU assembler (as), NASM uses Intel-style syntax instead of AT&T-style. Note: if you build ELFs (relocatable objects), you will need a separate linker such as GNU linker (ld) to produce a usable binary from them.
A portable x86 disassembler. Compared to GNU objdump, it can disassemble raw binary files with no header, symbol table or debug information present.
Displays network statistics such as current network connections, network interfaces and routing tables.
Runs the given program with a specific scheduling priority ("niceness"). Niceness ranges from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest priority), with 0 being default.

Allows you to run a program that is immune to hang up signals and output routed away or redirected to a file. The program can then run even when the host terminal is closed, the user logs out, or if it is run on a remote system and the connection is closed afterwards. It is often paired with an ampersand (&) to also send the command to the background.
Tells the Linux kernel about the presence and numbering of on-disk partitions.
Changes your user password, or if you are the root account, can change a given user's password.
Applies a patch file to an original file to update it with its contents. A patch file contains a line-by-line difference listing between two files produced by diff, git diff, or similar.
ELF binary patching.
Lists the process IDs for all processes that match the given regex pattern.
Lists the process IDs for all processes that match the given name.

Sends a signal to any processes selected by the given regex pattern. By default, it will try to gracefully terminate the process, but a given signal number (such as 9 for an immediate kill) can be given as well.

Reports the memory map of a given process. It provides the amount of memory used, proportional set sizes (PSS), dirty pages, permissions on map (mode), and mappings (file, anon/allocated or stack). All memory values are in kilobytes (KB).
Prints a list of running processes. It includes the process ID (PID), user name, time, and command.
Prints a process tree, optionally starting from a given user or process ID.
Shows the current working directory for the given process IDs.
A tool for listing, filtering, sorting and printing entries from a ctags tags file without needing a compatible editor.
Opens the Vim editor in restricted and read-only mode. This disables its shell escapes, external commands and ability to write.
Opens the Vim editor in restricted mode. This disables its shell escapes and external commands.

A terminal-based spreadsheet editor based on the original sc (spreadsheet calculator) but adds undo/redo, UTF-8, .xlsx workbook import/export, ODS export, clipboard integration, and Lua-based scripting support. It uses Vim-style keybinds.
An SCP client (a part of Dropbear) for remote file transfer.

Sets an extended attribute for the given filesystem object. Extended attributes are metadata that go beyond the standard attributes provided by the host filesystem, allowing more information to be associated with a given filesystem object.
A partitioning tool suited for automated and scripted use.

An ASCII text to 8-bit binary (and vice versa) converter. Modelled after Coreutils like base32, it plugs a hole for such a converter in the base command set. It accepts a filepath or standard input if no filepath is given.

A terminal-based file browser. It allows you to surf the file system with Vim-like controls, WASD or arrow keys, open text-based files with an installed editor of your choice, and inspect a file (if file is installed).

A shark-themed Linux fetch tool designed with speed, consistent output, and vintage hardware support in mind. It displays basic system and environment information in a summarised format. It can report the current username, hostname, operating system/distribution, kernel version, system uptime, number of installed packages, screens, desktop environment, window manager, terminal, console size, shell, CPU, GPUs, system memory, swap memory, root partition size, and local IP address.
EXPERIMENTAL. Starts the SHORKGUI graphical environment.
Provides help and reference information regarding SHORK and included software and tools. It provides a command database and list, guides, and cheatsheets.
A shark-themed take on the sl command that kindly pokes fun at making typos when trying to type "ls". When ran, an ASCII art shark moves across the terminal from left to right.

A vertical scrolling text screensaver. It is a minimalist, blue-themed take on CMatrix, a terminal program that provides "digital rain". Inspired by the 1999 film "The Matrix", the "droplets" are lines of blue characters that fall from the top of the terminal to the bottom, and are occasionally broken up.
An ncurses-based minesweeper game based on terminal-mines. You can customise the game’s difficulty by entering a width, height, and mine density of your choosing.

A shutdown helper that safely brings the system to a controlled halt before a manual power off. It is intended as an explicit utility that the user can call to sync write cache to help prevent data corruption or loss on especially older hardware when faced with a manual power off, then halts the system so the user can switch the power off without interrupting any active operations.

A shark-themed take on the cowsay command that outputs an ASCII art shark and a speech bubble containing a message of your choice. The message can be manually supplied or can be provided from another program's standard output (ie, using a pipe).
A settings program for changing SHORK's display resolution, keyboard layout (keymap), terminal PSF font, and terminal font colour.
An SSH client (a part of Dropbear) for remote login and command-line execution.
Used for initialising SCSI magnetic tape drive modes at system startup, when a tape driver module is loaded, or when a new tape driver is initialised using terminal commands.

Executes a given command to capture and trace its system calls and signals. It is a useful diagnosis and debugging tool one can run if a program fails unexpectedly, and/or without meaningful error messages or logs.

Allows you to log in and use the shell as another user without needing to log out of the current session. By default, it will try the root user, thus useful for quickly making administrative changes without needing to log out or switch consoles.

Single-user login. It is normally invoked by the init system when the host system goes into single-user mode (for example, for rescue or maintenance operations). If you run sulogin during a normal session, it functions similarly to using su to log in as the root user.
Used to stop memory paging/swapping on one or all swap-capable devices. If used and no swap devices are left online, the computer will be entirely reliant on system memory (RAM) for program memory.

Used to start memory paging/swapping on one or all swap-capable devices. Swapping allows fixed storage (hard disk drrive, solid-state drive, etc.) or removable storage (USB stick, etc.) to be used for program memory in addition to system memory (RAM). It is useful as a buffer for when free RAM runs low, although using swap memory will be much slower than RAM.

Commits any filesystem write operations that are currently cached. It is useful as an immediate and explicit way to ensure data is written to any disks/drives before powering off the computer, removing a drive, etc.

Creates, extracts or lists files from a given tar archive. It can also compress or decompress the archive based on the file extension or one of the explicit flags available. It also supports filtering files by name or glob pattern, changing directory before operating, and piping extracted files to another command.
Allows you to get or set the CPU affinity for a new program or an existing process via its ID.
A lightweight C compiler (configured to use musl).

Runs the given program until the given timeout, which will be terminated unless the program completes by itself. By default, it will try to gracefully terminate the program, but it can be told to immediately kill as well.

A terminal multiplexer that allows for multi-tasking and multi-viewing with just a single terminal. It allows you to create multiple "windows" to switch between without switching virtual terminals or opening a new window/tab in your terminal emulator, split said "windows" into multiple panes that can present terminal programs and output side-by-side, and quickly switch between them. Each tmux session can also be detached and reattached without losing what is open inside.

A process viewer that provides a real-time view of running processes and their CPU and memory usage. Besides comma-separated memory and CPU statistics and averages, it produces a table containing the process ID (PID), parent process ID (PPID), user, process state (STAT), virtual memory size in kilobytes (VSZ), VSZ as a percentage of total RAM (%VSZ), the last CPU core used, percentage of CPU time used (%CPU) and the executing command for each process that can fit into a single non-scrolling terminal.

Typically used to update the access and modification dates/times of one or more given files. It can also be used to create one or many empty files, as seen in some Linux books and tutorials, although this is often redundant.
Decompresses given Z archives, or Z-compressed standard input to standard output.
Converts a text file from using Unix-style line breaks (line feed) to using DOS-style line breaks (carriage return + line feed).
Decompresses given LZMA archives, or LZMA-compressed standard input to standard output. By default, it will replace the input files unless told otherwise.
Decompresses given LZO archives, or LZO-compressed standard input to standard output.
Decompresses given XZ archives, or XZ-compressed standard input to standard output. By default, it will replace the input files unless told otherwise.
Lists or extracts files from a given ZIP archive, with the option to specify a target directory or write to standard output.
Prints the users currently logged on.
Generates and prints a universally unique identifier (UUID), a 128-bit value for identification that is practically guaranteed to be unique.
Opens the Vim editor in read-only mode. This disables its ability to write.

An improved vi-style text editor that is highly extensible. Compared to regular vi, Vim supports syntax highlighting, folding, multiple buffers/windows/tabs, spell-checking, macros, undo trees and an scripting language called Vimscript. It also has a plugin system.
Opens the Vim editor in a mode that allows comparing two or more files side-by-side with their differences highlighted.
An interactive, self-paced tutorial that teaches you the basis of Vim using a disposable practice copy of the lesson file.

Reports system virtual memory, processes, CPU and I/O statistics. It displays columns for a runnable process count (r), I/O-bound blocked process count (b), swap memory used (swpd), idle memory (free), memory as buffers (buff), memory as cache (cache), memory swapped in from disk (si), memory swapped to disk (so), KiB received from a block device (bi), KiB sent to a block device (bo), interrupts per second (in), context switches per second (cs), user CPU time (us), system CPU time (sy), CPU idle time (id), time waiting for IO (wa), time stolen from a virtual machine (st), and time running KVM guest code (gu).
Shows which users are logged in, what ttyX they are logged into, how long they have been idling, and when they first logged in. Functions like who -H, always showing column headers.
Runs the given program periodically. By default, it will run every two seconds, unless a custom period is also given.
A non-interactive internet file downloader. It is often used to simply download a file with a given URL, although it can also be used as a web spider.
Locates the binary, source and manual page files for a given command.
Shows which users are logged in, what ttyX they are logged into, how long they have been idling, and when they first logged in. By default, it does not show column headers.
Prints the current user's name. Functions similarly to logname but uses the current effective user ID as its source.

Decompresses given XZ archives, or XZ-compressed standard input to standard output. By default, it will replace the input files unless told otherwise. Note: unlike XZ Utils' implementation of xz, BusyBox's version cannot compress any input.
Decompresses a given XZ archive to standard output. Functions like unxz -c.
Decompresses a given gzip archive to standard output. Functions like gunzip -c.
